lead: This unit shows how an Android screen is actually made: a tree of views arranged by layouts, a menu in the action bar, lists fed by adapters, and code that reacts to taps. You finish it able to build a working screen in XML or in Java, and to keep that screen correct when the phone is rotated. Every idea is tied to a small screen you could build in one lab session.
about: The unit is about the Android user interface, layer by layer. Chapter 3.1 shows the view tree and the layout managers that position children, with dp and weights. Chapter 3.2 handles what happens when the phone turns and the activity is destroyed and recreated. Chapter 3.3 puts the action bar and menus on top of the layout. Chapter 3.4 covers the everyday widgets, text, buttons, spinners and list views, and the adapters that feed lists. Chapter 3.5 adds images, progress and scrolling views. Chapter 3.6 builds the same screens in code and wires listeners to touch events. Activities, intents and fragments come from Unit 2; saving data for good is Unit 4.

chapters.idea: An Android screen is a tree of views, and a ViewGroup called a layout decides where each child sits and how big it is.
chapters.depth: Start with the split: a View draws something, a ViewGroup is a View that holds children. The activity window holds one root ViewGroup; every screen is a tree under it. Cover the shared View attributes: android:id (@+id/name), layout_width and layout_height (match_parent, wrap_content, a fixed dp value), padding (inside) vs margin (outside), background, visibility, enabled. Then the layouts: LinearLayout (orientation, layout_weight, weightSum, the 0dp rule), RelativeLayout (layout_below, layout_toRightOf, layout_alignParentRight), FrameLayout (children stack, later ones on top), TableLayout (rows, stretchColumns), ConstraintLayout (constraints to parent and to siblings), GridLayout. Units: dp is density-independent, px = dp × dpi ÷ 160, sp is for text so the user's font size applies. Resource references @string, @dimen, @color live in res/values. Some syllabi call this 'designing by declaration' or call layouts 'screen containers'.

figure.aria: A horizontal LinearLayout of width 360 dp with three weighted buttons whose widths work out to 60, 120 and 180 dp.

chapters.example: A horizontal LinearLayout is match_parent wide on a screen 360 dp wide. It holds three buttons, each with layout_width = 0dp and layout_weight = 1, 2 and 3. Find each button's width in dp, and in pixels on a 480 dpi screen. Answer: the weights add to 6, so one weight unit is 360 ÷ 6 = 60 dp. The buttons are 1 × 60 = 60 dp, 2 × 60 = 120 dp and 3 × 60 = 180 dp, and 60 + 120 + 180 = 360 dp. Density = 480 ÷ 160 = 3, so in pixels they are 180 px, 360 px and 540 px.
chapters.trap: gravity centres a layout's own children, while layout_gravity places that view inside its parent; swapping them is the most common layout bug. Second trap: weights only share space cleanly when the child's width is 0dp. With match_parent the child already asks for the whole row and the arithmetic gives surprising widths.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2: activities and the activity life cycle, because a layout is inflated inside onCreate.
chapters.leave: Fragments and specialized fragments to Unit 2; keeping the layout's state across rotation to 3.2; filling views from a database to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Rotating the phone is a configuration change, and Android answers it by destroying and recreating the activity, so any UI state you care about must be saved and restored.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this as a full topic, so keep it shorter. When the device rotates, the screen size and orientation qualifiers change and Android rebuilds the activity: onPause → onStop → onDestroy, then onCreate → onStart → onResume on the new layout. Cover onSaveInstanceState(Bundle) and onRestoreInstanceState, and the fact that views with an id save their own state (an EditText with an id keeps its text automatically). Cover alternative resources: res/layout-land/, res/values-land/, res/values-sw600dp/. Cover the escape hatch android:configChanges="orientation|screenSize" with onConfigurationChanged, and the two surviving-state options: a retained fragment and a ViewModel. Mention that the Bundle is small and parcelable, not a database.

figure.title: Rotation: activity recreated
figure.aria: A portrait activity runs, gets paused, stopped and destroyed on rotation, then is created again with a Bundle and returns to resumed in landscape.

chapters.example: An activity keeps an int field count and a TextView shows "Taps: 7" after seven taps on a button. The phone rotates from 1080 × 1920 portrait to 1920 × 1080 landscape. (a) What shows with no saving code? (b) With onSaveInstanceState putting count in the Bundle and onCreate reading it back? (c) With android:configChanges="orientation|screenSize" declared? Answer: (a) the count field is 0, because a new activity object was built, so the label reads "Taps: 0"; (b) the Bundle carries 7 into the new onCreate, so the label reads "Taps: 7"; (c) the activity is not destroyed, onConfigurationChanged runs instead, and the field still holds 7 for free.
chapters.trap: onSaveInstanceState is not called when the user presses Back or when you call finish(), so it is for transient screen state only, never for data you must keep. Second trap: android:configChanges hides the problem but does not give you the landscape layout, so the UI stays stretched.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 activity life cycle; 3.1 layouts, since rotation inflates a second layout tree.
chapters.leave: Preferences, files and SQLite for real persistence to Unit 4; ViewModel internals to an architecture course.

chapters.idea: The action bar is a strip owned by the activity, and its buttons and overflow list come from a menu XML that the activity inflates and handles by item id.
chapters.depth: Cover the action bar contents: app icon, title, action buttons, overflow (three dots). Modern apps use a Toolbar with setSupportActionBar(toolbar), but the menu API is unchanged. Menus live in res/menu/main.xml: a <menu> with <item> children carrying android:id, android:title, android:icon, app:showAsAction, android:orderInCategory, and optional <group> or sub-<menu>. Life cycle of a menu: onCreateOptionsMenu inflates it, onPrepareOptionsMenu changes it, onOptionsItemSelected consumes the click and returns true. showAsAction values: always, ifRoom, never, withText. Also cover the Up arrow (android.R.id.home) and the difference between Up and Back, context menus (registerForContextMenu, onCreateContextMenu, onContextItemSelected) and the floating PopupMenu. Some syllabi call this the app bar.

figure.aria: A menu resource with five items, three fitting on the bar and two falling into the overflow list.

chapters.example: A toolbar has room for 3 action slots. Its menu XML has five items: Search with showAsAction="always"; Share, Edit and Delete with showAsAction="ifRoom"; Settings with showAsAction="never". Which items appear on the bar, and how many go to overflow? Answer: Search takes slot 1 always. The ifRoom items are placed in declaration order into the 2 free slots: Share takes slot 2, Edit takes slot 3, Delete does not fit. Settings never shows on the bar. Overflow therefore holds Delete and Settings, 2 items, and the bar shows 3.
chapters.trap: showAsAction is a custom attribute, so it must be written app:showAsAction with the app namespace; android:showAsAction is silently ignored on a Toolbar and everything drops into overflow. Second trap: returning false from onOptionsItemSelected makes the system fall through, so the item looks dead.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 layouts, because the action bar sits above the activity's content layout.
chapters.leave: Intents fired from a menu item to Unit 2; a full settings screen backed by preferences to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Each basic view has its own input model, and list-style views never hold the data themselves: an adapter turns the data list into row views on demand.
chapters.depth: Cover TextView (textSize in sp, textColor, maxLines), EditText (hint, inputType such as textEmailAddress or numberPassword), Button and ImageButton, CheckBox, RadioButton inside a RadioGroup so only one is checked, Switch and ToggleButton, AutoCompleteTextView. Then pickers: Spinner with android:entries or a custom adapter, setOnItemSelectedListener, getSelectedItemPosition, getSelectedItem; DatePicker, TimePicker, NumberPicker. Then ListView: ArrayAdapter with android.R.layout.simple_list_item_1, setOnItemClickListener with (parent, view, position, id), getItemAtPosition, and recycling: only the visible rows exist, so getView is called with a recycled convertView (ViewHolder pattern). Make the adapter idea explicit: data list → adapter.getItemView → one row view.

figure.title: ListView adapter
figure.aria: Five list items held in the adapter, with index 2 marked as the tapped row.

chapters.example: A ListView is bound by an ArrayAdapter to five items shown with simple_list_item_1: Fig, Plum, Pear, Kiwi, Lime. The user taps the third row. Give the arguments of onItemClick and say what getItemAtPosition(2) returns. Then the same five entries fill a Spinner whose default selection is index 0; after setSelection(3), what do getSelectedItemPosition() and getSelectedItem() return? Answer: the callback is onItemClick(parent, view, position, id) with position = 2, and getItemAtPosition(2) returns "Pear". For the Spinner, getSelectedItemPosition() returns 3 and getSelectedItem() returns "Kiwi".
chapters.trap: position is the index in the adapter, so it shifts as soon as you add a header view, while id is the row id the adapter reports; treating id as the index gives wrong rows. Second trap: after changing the backing list you must call notifyDataSetChanged(), otherwise the screen keeps the old rows.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 layouts; Unit 2 activities, since listeners are set in onCreate.
chapters.leave: Custom row XML and ViewHolder performance tuning to a later reading; feeding lists from a database with a CursorAdapter to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Beyond text and buttons, Android gives a family of views for images, progress and scrolling, and each one has a rule that decides how content is measured and scaled.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this group, so keep it shorter. Cover ImageView: android:src vs android:background, scaleType (centerCrop, fitCenter, fitXY, center, centerInside, matrix), adjustViewBounds. Cover ImageButton, GridView with a BaseAdapter, and WebView (loadUrl, needs the INTERNET permission). Cover feedback views: ProgressBar in determinate (setProgress) and indeterminate mode, SeekBar with setOnSeekBarChangeListener, RatingBar with setNumStars and setRating. Cover ScrollView and HorizontalScrollView, which hold exactly one child. Mention VideoView in one line only.

figure.aria: Four families of views stacked from media views at the top down to the basic widgets from the previous chapter.

chapters.example: An ImageView is 400 px wide and 300 px high. The bitmap is 200 px wide and 600 px high. Find the drawn size and the crop for scaleType fitCenter and for centerCrop. Answer: fitCenter uses scale = min(400/200, 300/600) = min(2, 0.5) = 0.5, so the bitmap is drawn at 100 × 300 px and centred, leaving (400 − 100)/2 = 150 px blank on each side. centerCrop uses scale = max(2, 0.5) = 2, so the bitmap is drawn at 400 × 1200 px and then cropped to 400 × 300: 1200 − 300 = 900 px of height is lost, 450 px from the top and 450 px from the bottom.
chapters.trap: fitXY stretches the bitmap to the view box and ignores the aspect ratio, which is why photos look fat. Second trap: scaleType acts on src; a background drawable is always stretched to the view bounds and ignores scaleType.
chapters.prereq: 3.4 basic views and the adapter idea, which GridView reuses.
chapters.leave: Downloading and caching images to Unit 5; WebView JavaScript bridges and media playback to other units.

chapters.idea: Every XML layout can be built in Java instead, and a touch becomes a callback through one fixed path: dispatchTouchEvent, then onTouchEvent, then performClick, then your onClick.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach building the UI in code; it is worth knowing because every XML attribute has a setter. Cover new TextView(this), setText, setTextSize, setPadding, setId, setLayoutParams(new LinearLayout.LayoutParams(0, LinearLayout.LayoutParams.WRAP_CONTENT, 1f)), addView, then setContentView(root). Cover converting dp to px with getResources().getDisplayMetrics().density. Then events: android:onClick="onButtonClick" in XML needing a public void method with one View parameter; the anonymous button.setOnClickListener(new View.OnClickListener(){ onClick(View v){...} }); the activity itself implementing View.OnClickListener. Show the dispatch path and where returning false from onTouchEvent matters. Add TextWatcher (afterTextChanged) as the notification for text fields, and Log.d(tag, message) to confirm a listener fired.

figure.title: A tap becomes a callback
figure.aria: A finger tap travels from dispatchTouchEvent down to onTouchEvent, performClick and finally the listener's onClick method.

chapters.example: Build a horizontal LinearLayout in code, match_parent wide on a 360 dp screen, holding three buttons each with layout width 0 and weight 1. Button i gets id 100 + i, and each button gets the same OnClickListener. The user taps the second button. What is each button's width, and what does the listener receive? Answer: the weights are equal, so 360 ÷ 3 = 120 dp each; at density 3 that is 360 px each. The listener receives the tapped View v, v.getId() returns 101, and (v.getId() − 100) = 1 gives the index of the tapped button.
chapters.trap: A view created in code has no LayoutParams until you set them; addView(view) with no params falls back to wrap_content and your weights silently do nothing. Second trap: the XML onClick method must be public, return void and take exactly one View argument, or the app crashes on the first tap.
chapters.prereq: 3.1 layouts for LayoutParams and weights; 3.4 for listeners on lists and buttons.
chapters.leave: The debugger, breakpoints and build tooling to Unit 2; fragments created in code to Unit 2.

links: rotation rebuilds the same layout tree from a second resource
the action bar sits above the activity's content layout
layouts exist to hold the basic views at fixed sizes and weights
a layout-land version must restore the list's selected row
menu clicks arrive as listener callbacks in code
the same widget family grows to images, progress and scrolling
adapters and click listeners can be wired without XML
custom view trees are often built in code to control measuring
